content.headline: About EduInsights
content.subhead: A blog by educators and technologists exploring the future of learning

content.content:
## Our Mission

EduInsights was founded in 2020 to bridge the gap between educational research and practical implementation. Too often, evidence-based teaching practices stay locked in academic journals while ed-tech products are built on assumptions rather than data.

We believe better tools and better teaching methods come from:

- **Evidence-based thinking**: Starting with research, not opinions
- **Practical application**: Showing how to actually implement ideas
- **Honest evaluation**: Calling out what doesn't work
- **Open sharing**: No paywalls, no gatekeeping

## Our Writers

We're a team of educators, researchers, and product builders who've worked at universities, ed-tech companies, and schools. We've collectively:

- Taught over 100,000 students
- Built learning platforms serving millions
- Published research in peer-reviewed journals
- Designed courses with 90%+ completion rates

## Topics We Cover

- Learning science and cognitive psychology
- Course design and instructional methods
- Ed-tech product development
- Student engagement and motivation
- Assessment and feedback design
- Accessibility and inclusive education
- Business models and sustainability

## Get in Touch

We'd love to hear from you:

- **Email**: hello@eduinsights.blog
- **Twitter**: [@eduinsights](https://twitter.com/eduinsights)
- **Newsletter**: [Subscribe here](/subscribe)
- **Pitch an article**: editors@eduinsights.blog

meta.title: The Spacing Effect: Why Cramming Doesn't Work

content.content:
# The Spacing Effect: Why Cramming Doesn't Work

*Dr. Sarah Chen · Jan 2, 2025 · 8 min read*

**Research shows that distributed practice dramatically improves long-term retention. Here's how to apply spacing principles in online courses—and what ed-tech platforms get wrong about review schedules.**

## The Problem with Cramming

Every student knows the drill: exam next week, better study everything tonight. It feels productive—you're reviewing dozens of concepts, taking frantic notes, highlighting textbooks.

But here's the uncomfortable truth: **most of what you cram is forgotten within 48 hours**.

The "spacing effect" is one of the most robust findings in learning science. Distributing practice over time leads to dramatically better long-term retention than massed practice (cramming), even when total study time is identical.

## The Research

Cepeda et al. (2006) analyzed 317 experiments on spacing effects spanning over a century. Their meta-analysis found:

- Spaced practice improves retention by **10-30%** on average
- Effects are stronger for complex material
- Benefits persist for months or years
- Optimal spacing depends on retention interval

### Optimal Spacing Schedules

For material you need to remember:

- **1 week later**: Review after 1-2 days
- **1 month later**: Review after 1 week
- **1 year later**: Review after 1 month

The key principle: spacing should expand over time (expanding rehearsal).

## What Ed-Tech Gets Wrong

Most course platforms completely ignore spacing effects:

### ❌ Linear Content Delivery

"Complete Module 1, then Module 2, then Module 3."

Students never see Module 1 material again after they finish it.

### ❌ End-of-Course Reviews

"Review everything right before the final exam."

This is literally massed practice.

### ❌ Optional Review Quizzes

"Click here if you want to review."

Students don't know what they need to review until they forget it (too late).

## What Actually Works

### ✅ Interleaved Content

Mix old topics into new lessons. When teaching JavaScript loops (Module 3), include problems requiring variables (Module 1) and conditionals (Module 2).

### ✅ Scheduled Retrieval Practice

Force recall at expanding intervals:

- Day 1: Learn concept
- Day 2: Quiz on concept
- Day 7: Quiz again
- Day 21: Quiz again
- Day 60: Quiz again

### ✅ Adaptive Spacing Algorithms

Use spaced repetition software (SRS) principles:

- Short intervals for weak items
- Long intervals for mastered items
- Dynamic adjustment based on performance

## Implementation Guide

Here's how to build spacing into your online course:

### 1. Create a Review Item Bank

For every lesson, create 5-10 review questions covering key concepts. Store these in a separate bank.

### 2. Schedule Automatic Reviews

Every 3-4 lessons, insert a review quiz drawing from previous lessons:

- 40% from most recent lesson
- 30% from 2-3 lessons ago
- 20% from 4-6 lessons ago
- 10% from 7+ lessons ago

### 3. Use Cumulative Assignments

Every project should require knowledge from multiple modules. Don't let students compartmentalize.

### 4. Build Review into Communication

Weekly emails to students:

> "This week we covered React hooks. Can you still explain the difference between var, let, and const from Week 2? If not, review this 2-minute video."

## Example: Course Redesign

**Before (Linear)**
```
Week 1: Variables
Week 2: Conditionals
Week 3: Loops
Week 4: Functions
Week 5: Final Project
```

**After (Spaced)**
```
Week 1: Variables
Week 2: Conditionals + Variables Quiz
Week 3: Loops + Conditionals Quiz
Week 4: Functions + All Topics Quiz
Week 5: Project (uses everything) + Weekly Mini-Reviews
```

## Measuring Impact

I implemented spaced review in my data science course (n=240 students):

- **Before**: 67% average on delayed retention test (1 month post-course)
- **After**: 84% average on same test
- **Student feedback**: 92% found reviews helpful (vs. 43% who found end-of-course review helpful)

## Common Objections

**"But this makes courses longer!"**

No—it makes them more effective. Same content, better sequencing. You're adding 5-minute quizzes, not new lessons.

**"Students will complain about repetition."**

Frame it correctly: "Spaced practice is proven to improve retention. You'll thank me later." Students appreciate it when it works.

**"My platform doesn't support this."**

You don't need fancy software. A spreadsheet of review questions and manual quiz insertion works fine.

## Conclusion

The spacing effect isn't controversial—it's one of the most replicated findings in psychology. Yet most online courses completely ignore it.

Stop organizing content linearly. Start designing for retention.

Your students' future selves will thank you.

---

## References

- Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. *Psychological Bulletin, 132*(3), 354-380.
- Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. *Science, 319*(5865), 966-968.
